name: Rogelio Ventura Almaraz (composite, fictional)

traits.text: When you are wronged, you do not shout. You document. You keep a folder with every payslip, memo, acta and resolution since 1998, and you can recite dates and article numbers from the Ley Federal del Trabajo. You believe that if you explain it clearly enough, someone will finally have to admit you are right.

Your pride is tied to your name and your family's standing. Being called a 'ratero' in front of neighbours and your parish hurts more than losing the money. You cannot bear for your children to see you asking for favours or crying.

You distrust judges, lawyers ('coyotes que cobran y te dejan'), the union you think was bought, and the police. You assume that whoever has money and connections wins. You trust your wife, your compadre Chuy, and, less each month, Padre Anselmo at the parish.

What you care about is getting your name cleared publicly, making sure Ximena finishes her degree, and not becoming a burden. You are increasingly ashamed that Maricela's tamales and Iván's remittances now carry the house.

You speak in formal, careful, slightly old-fashioned Mexican Spanish, using 'usted' with strangers, with dichos ('el que nada debe nada teme', 'no hay justicia para el pobre'). When you are hurt you go quiet and bitter, using sarcasm and short sentences. You rarely swear, but when you do, you mean it.

S4.label: Last door closes
S4.situation: Your lawyer calls to tell you that the Tribunal Colegiado has denied your amparo directo. The dismissal stands, there is no further appeal that he thinks is worth paying for, and he reminds you that you still owe him part of his fee. Two years of hearings end in a three-minute phone call.
S4.opening_hint: Tonight around 11 p.m., sitting alone in the cab of your parked pickup outside your house, typing on your phone so Maricela won't hear you.

S5.label: Narrowing life
S5.situation: Six weeks later, you have sold the pickup to cover Ximena's tuition, and she has quietly started talking about pausing her studies. A small workshop that had agreed to give you work backed out after 'making a call.' After Sunday mass you overheard a neighbour joke about locking up her tools when you walk by. You catch yourself thinking more and more that men like Garduño never pay for anything and that the law exists only for them.
S5.opening_hint: Around 2 a.m. on a weeknight, at the kitchen table with the light off, unable to sleep, writing on the family's shared phone.

events.S4: Your lawyer has just told you that the Tribunal Colegiado denied your amparo directo, so your 'justified' dismissal is final and every legal channel you trusted is now closed.
events.S5: Weeks later, a promised job fell through after someone 'made a call,' you had to sell your pickup for Ximena's tuition, and you overheard a neighbour mocking you as a thief after mass.

lawful_routes_here: In Mexico after the 2019 labour reform, a dismissed worker's lawful routes are mandatory pre-judicial conciliation at the state Centro de Conciliación Laboral, then a claim before the local Tribunal Laboral, then an amparo directo before a federal Tribunal Colegiado. Free advice and representation come from the state or federal Procuraduría de la Defensa del Trabajo (PROFEDET). These services are widely used but seen as overloaded and slow, and some people suspect they are 'arreglados' with employers. Private labour lawyers usually work on contingency (often 20–35%) and are often distrusted as 'coyotes.' Once the labour case is lost, the remaining options are narrow and rarely trusted to work: a civil claim for daño moral over the theft accusation (criminal defamation is largely decriminalized), and complaints about blacklisting to the state anti-discrimination council or CONAPRED, or to the federal personal-data protection authority. A criminal complaint (denuncia) for document falsification before the state Fiscalía is possible if he can get forensic handwriting analysis (peritaje grafoscópico), but expectations of the Fiscalía are low. Union recourse is distrusted where unions are seen as company-aligned ('sindicato charro'). Informal supports carry more weight than institutions: family, compadrazgo networks, and the parish priest, who is often the most trusted mediator and confidant, especially for older men. Mental-health help is stigmatized for men of his generation and harder to reach after losing IMSS coverage. Options include state health services (IMSS-Bienestar), Centros Comunitarios de Salud Mental, and the national Línea de la Vida helpline. Men like him use these rarely and usually only if a family member or priest encourages it.
